segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now in those days, as the disciples were multiplying, there was grumbling from the Hellenists against the Hebrews, because their widows were being overlooked in the daily serving.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the Twelve summoned the whole body of the disciples and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “It is not acceptable for us to abandon the word of God to serve at tables.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So, brothers and sisters, look for seven men from among you who are well spoken of, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom we will appoint over this duty.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the service of the word.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The proposal pleased the whole body, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte from Antioch.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: These they stood before the apostles, and after praying they laid their hands on them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the word of God kept growing, and the number of the disciples in Jerusalem multiplied greatly, and a large crowd of the priests were becoming obedient to the faith.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then some of those from what was called the Synagogue of the Freedmen, Cyrenians and Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia, rose up and began arguing with Stephen,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but they were not able to stand against the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then they secretly put men up to saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We have heard him speaking blasphemous words against Moses and God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They stirred up the people, the elders and the scribes, and coming upon him they seized him and brought him to the council.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They put forward false witnesses who said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This man never stops speaking words against the holy place and the law,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: for we have heard him say that this Jesus the Nazarene will destroy this place and change the customs that Moses handed down to us.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And all who were sitting in the council, gazing intently at him, saw that his face was like the face of an angel.

notes.note: Both groups are Jewish followers of Jesus in Jerusalem. On the usual view the Hellenists were Jews whose first language was Greek, many of them from the diaspora, while the Hebrews spoke Aramaic or Hebrew. The word is rare and its exact scope is debated, but a difference of language and culture within the community is the standard explanation.

Most translations have 'distribution', which fits the situation (regular support for widows, in food or money). The Greek noun is the ordinary word for service, and Luke repeats it deliberately: the widows are missed in the daily 'serving', the Twelve will not 'serve' at tables, and they devote themselves to the 'service' of the word. The rendering keeps that thread visible.

The word for table was used both of a dining table and of a money-changer's or banker's counter. The phrase may therefore mean serving food at meals or administering the funds from which the widows were supported. Most interpreters think of meals, but the financial sense is possible.

The Greek plural was the normal way to address a mixed group and did not exclude women; here the whole body of disciples is being addressed. Many translations keep 'brothers'. The seven to be chosen, by contrast, are specified as men with a word that means adult males.

A proselyte was a Gentile who had fully converted to Judaism. Nicolaus is the only one of the seven so described, which implies the others were Jews by birth. All seven names are Greek, which is often taken as a sign that they came from the Hellenist group, though Greek names were common among Jews generally.

notes.phrase: after praying they laid their hands on them
notes.traditional: and when they had prayed, they laid their hands on them
notes.note: The Greek does not change subject, so grammatically the ones who pray and lay on hands could be the whole community that chose the seven. Most interpreters take the apostles to be the subject, as the nearest noun and in line with verse 3. The translation leaves the wording as open as the Greek.

notes.phrase: the Synagogue of the Freedmen, Cyrenians and Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia
notes.traditional: the synagogue of the Libertines (Freedmen), and Cyrenians, and Alexandrians, and of them of Cilicia and of Asia
notes.note: The grammar leaves it unclear how many synagogues are meant: one with members from all these places, two (as rendered here, following the two groupings in the Greek), or as many as five. 'Freedmen' is a Latin loanword for former slaves or their descendants, probably Jews whose families had been taken to Rome as captives and later released. Asia here is the Roman province in what is now western Turkey.

The Greek could mean the Holy Spirit or Stephen's own spirit, that is, the force with which he spoke. Since Stephen has just been described as full of the Holy Spirit, the translation takes it as the Spirit; translations are divided.
This is the Sanhedrin, the supreme Jewish council in Jerusalem, presided over by the high priest. It is the same body that had tried Jesus and had recently flogged the apostles.

The holy place is the Jerusalem temple. The charge that Jesus would destroy it resembles the accusation Mark and Matthew report at Jesus's own trial, which they too attribute to false witnesses. Some manuscripts read 'this holy place'; the text translated here lacks 'this'.

candidates.reason: The plural address to mixed groups recurs throughout Acts and the letters, and translations split between 'brothers' and 'brothers and sisters'; readers will notice inconsistency.
The διακον- word group is rendered variously as service, ministry and distribution, and here the repetition is deliberate; one policy is needed across the New Testament.
Translations vary between 'council' and 'Sanhedrin' across the Gospels and Acts, and the same body should have the same name throughout.
'Scribe' suggests a copyist to modern readers, whereas the word denotes experts in the law; it is frequent in the Gospels and Acts and needs one decision.
It occurs in the Gospels and Acts alongside Ναζαρηνός and is rendered variously as 'of Nazareth', 'the Nazarene' or 'the Nazorean'; a single policy is needed.
